oil.summary: Crude markets delivered a landmark session as Brent broke back through $100/bbl — the first time in nearly two months — closing at $100.51, up 6.85% on the day and +30.4% over the past month. WTI settled at $92.28, adding 6.31%. The catalyst is unambiguous: Houthi forces struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia, and ongoing U.S.-Iran military exchanges show no sign of de-escalation, with Trump threatening further strikes after three U.S. soldiers were killed. Kazakhstan's export capacity is simultaneously being squeezed by Ukrainian drone strikes on pipeline infrastructure. On the sanctions front, the EU froze the Russian oil price cap adjustment for one year while adding measures targeting tankers and refining. RBOB gasoline diverged, falling 2.81%, suggesting some demand-side anxiety at the pump level offsetting the supply shock bid.
drivers: Houthi strikes on two Saudi tankers and declaration of a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia drove acute Red Sea supply-route risk
Active U.S.-Iran military conflict with no ceasefire signals; Iran pledging oil blockade continuation pushed geopolitical premium sharply higher
EU sanctions freeze on Russian price cap plus Kazakhstan export disruptions tightened the broader supply picture simultaneously

gas.summary: Natural gas markets showed a clear transatlantic divergence today. Henry Hub eased 0.44% to $2.912/MMBtu, remaining under pressure with a one-month decline of 7.47%, suggesting ample North American supply buffers the Middle East shock for now. European TTF slipped 1.08% on the session to €61.86/MWh but remains elevated — up 47.24% over the past month — as the war premium and supply rerouting costs stay embedded in European pricing. Politically, the EU struck a compromise allowing Russian gas cargoes to stay exempt from the latest sanctions package, with Greek LNG operator Dynagas specifically carved out after Athens lobbied against measures it said would harm its fleet. Meanwhile, LNG importers are reportedly seeking to renegotiate lower prices from Qatar and UAE, as the war has eroded those exporters' traditional pricing leverage.
drivers: EU sanctions deal exempts Russian gas cargoes and grants a specific carve-out for Greek LNG operator Dynagas following political pressure from Athens
TTF remains 47% above month-ago levels as Middle East conflict sustains European supply risk premium, despite today's modest pullback
LNG importers pushing back on Qatar and UAE pricing, with war-driven market disruption weakening traditional Gulf exporter negotiating power

power.summary: The power and carbon complex offered a mixed picture with limited sector-specific headline flow today. EU carbon EUAs fell 2.64% to $79.61/EUA, pulling back despite the broader energy price surge, though the one-week gain of 6.47% shows the conflict's footprint on the carbon market. TTF's near-50% monthly rally is the dominant cost input stressing European power generation economics. On the structural side, Ember Energy flagged significant untapped potential in hybrid renewable projects co-located on existing hydropower sites in Europe. India announced a target of five domestically built small modular reactors by 2033, a longer-dated but notable nuclear ambition signal. U.S. refinery utilization hitting 96.2% reflects the tightness cascading through global fuel markets, which indirectly pressures power generation feedstock costs.
drivers: EU EUAs retreated 2.64% on the session despite elevated TTF, suggesting some carbon demand softness even as power generation costs remain stressed
India targets five domestically built SMRs by 2033, signaling growing state-level commitment to nuclear capacity outside the West
Ember Energy report highlights hybrid hydropower co-development as a near-term European renewable upside opportunity amid the energy security push
